The partition key determines how items are distributed across physical partitions; items that share a partition key value form a logical partition so related data stays co‑located, making queries within that logical partition efficient and scoping transactions to a single logical partition [1]. A good partition key has high cardinality and spreads storage and request volume evenly to avoid hot partitions [2].

Use Azure Service Bus queues as the messaging layer and run your worker in Azure Container Apps with a KEDA scale rule on the Service Bus queue depth. Service Bus provides fully managed queues for competing consumers and supports work-distribution patterns (with retries, per-message TTL, and dead-lettering) [3][1][5]. A KEDA scale rule on Service Bus queue depth is the canonical pattern to scale workers out as the queue deepens and back to zero when it drains [2]. Azure Container Apps uses KEDA-based autoscaling and can scale to zero replicas so no compute charges accrue while the app is at zero [8].

The Reliability pillar recommends deploying redundant instances across fault domains so no single failure takes a workload down [2]. Availability zones are exactly such fault domains: they are physically separate datacenters with independent power, cooling, and networking, and zone‑redundant deployments keep a workload available when a single zone fails [2]. For example, Container Apps can spread replicas across zones so loss of one zone does not take the app down [1]. This matches the Reliability principle to “design for failure” and to analyze failure modes and limit blast radius using such mitigations [3][5].
